title: India's Current Account: Why a Surprise Surplus in Q4 FY26 Matters
description: India recorded a healthy $7.1 billion (₹59,200 crore approx.) current account surplus in January-March 2026 (Q4 FY26). This means the country earned more fore.

faq.q: What is the Balance of Payments (BoP)?
faq.a: The Balance of Payments (BoP) is a comprehensive record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world over a specific period. The Current Account is a major component of the BoP, along with the Capital Account.

faq.q: What helps India finance its Current Account Deficit?
faq.a: If India runs a CAD, it needs to be financed by inflows in the Capital Account. This includes foreign direct investment (FDI), foreign portfolio investment (FPI), external commercial borrowings (loans from abroad), and non-resident Indian (NRI) deposits. If these inflows are not enough, the country has to use its foreign exchange reserves.

faq.q: What is considered a "manageable" CAD for India?
faq.a: Economists generally consider a Current Account Deficit of around 2-2.5% of GDP as sustainable for a developing economy like India. Our current full-year CAD of 0.6% of GDP is well below this threshold, indicating a healthy external sector.

faq.q: How do remittances from NRIs help India's current account?
faq.a: Remittances are a significant source of foreign currency inflow for India. They are part of the "secondary income" component of the current account and directly reduce the overall deficit or contribute to a surplus, as seen in Q4 FY26.

faq.q: What is the main reason for India's merchandise trade deficit?
faq.a: India typically runs a merchandise trade deficit primarily due to its high import bill for crude oil, which is essential for our energy needs, and also for items like gold, electronics, and machinery.
